`ln` only links one target at a time. Your command expands `/data/sdext2/app/*` into many arguments, so `ln` fails.

Use a loop and create each symlink separately, for example:

`for i in /data/sdext2/app/*; do ln -s "$i" /data/app/$(basename "$i"); done`

If you’re linking into `/data/app`, make sure the destination names don’t already exist there, or `ln` will report “File exists.”

Android does support symbolic links, but only on filesystems that allow them. You cannot create symlinks on filesystems like FAT or RFS. If your device’s partition uses a supported filesystem such as ext2, ext3, ext4, or yaffs2, you should be able to create one with `ln -s` from a terminal emulator.

To check whether an Android phone is running well for 3G, try this order:

2. Force 3G only: dial *#*#4636#*#* → Phone Information → select WCDMA only.

4. Try a different SIM that has working 3G.

6. If the issue still remains, have the phone checked for a hardware defect.

The supported method here is to unpack the boot image first, then extract the ramdisk separately.

If `split_bootimg.pl` says “Android Magic not found”, use `unpack-bootimg.pl` instead. It should produce files like `boot.img-kernel.gz` and `boot.img-ramdisk.cpio.gz`.

Then extract the ramdisk with:

`gzip -dc boot.img-ramdisk.cpio.gz | cpio -i`

It’s best to do this inside a separate directory, such as `ramdisk/`, to keep things organized.

If you later modify the ramdisk, the reverse process shown is:

`mkbootfs ramdisk/ | gzip > my_new_ramdisk.gz`

If you have physical access to the device, you can install it with Android SDK tools using ADB:

1. Install the Android SDK tools.
2. Install the phone’s USB drivers.
3. Enable USB debugging on the phone.
4. Connect the phone by USB.
5. In Terminal/Command Prompt, go to the SDK `platform-tools` folder.
6. Run:

`adb install path_to_apk\your_app.apk`

This installs the app from the APK file. However, it still copies the APK onto the device, so a knowledgeable user may be able to retrieve it afterward.

If it’s a system app APK, you generally can’t install it through the normal installer. You need root/ADB access and copy the APK into the system partition, such as /system/app or, on Android 4.3+, /system/priv-app.

Typical steps:
1. Remount /system as read-write:
adb shell
su
mount -o rw,remount /system

or:
adb root
adb remount

2. Push/move the APK to the system folder:
adb push my-app.apk /sdcard/
adb shell
su
mv /sdcard/my-app.apk /system/app
(or /system/priv-app)

3. Set permissions to rw-r--r--:
chmod 644 /system/app/my-app.apk

4. Reboot the device:
adb reboot

An AOSP ROM is built from Google’s unmodified Android source. A stock ROM is the manufacturer’s version of Android that comes with the device or is released as an official update.

In practice, stock ROMs include the maker’s changes and device-specific support, while AOSP is more generic and closer to “vanilla” Android.

An AOSP ROM is built from Android’s open-source code base. It’s the “pure” Android source, but it does not include closed-source pieces like many hardware drivers or Google’s proprietary apps/services.

A stock ROM usually means the manufacturer’s official ROM that came with the device or was delivered via OTA updates. It’s typically based on AOSP, but includes device-specific drivers and often manufacturer modifications, and may also include Google or vendor apps.

So, in short: AOSP = open-source Android base; stock ROM = the device maker’s official, usually customized build.

LOST.DIR is a folder Android uses as storage for files recovered after a boot, usually after the SD card was corrupted or not safely removed. It can be safely deleted, but the system may recreate it if needed. To help prevent it from appearing, avoid SD card corruption: always eject before removal, don’t remove it while files are being modified, and don’t remove it while the device is on. Using a higher-class SD card may also reduce the problem.

LOST.DIR is a special folder used by filesystem repair/check tools. It’s where corrupted or orphaned files can be placed when a drive is checked. Android also creates this directory during its filesystem check and puts files there that it believes are corrupt.

LOST.DIR is a folder Android creates to hold recovered files after a boot or SD-card corruption. You can safely delete it, but if it keeps coming back, it usually means the SD card is being corrupted or removed/mounted unsafely.

To reduce it: always eject before removing the card, don’t remove it while files are being modified, and don’t pull it while the phone is on. If you’re already doing that, the card may be partially incompatible; using a higher-class SD card may help.

“Root access required” means you need administrator-level access on the device’s operating system before you can do the task. In the context here, flashing a custom ROM usually does not require root if you use other methods, such as a manufacturer/carrier flashing tool, a signed update package in recovery/bootloader, or direct writing via a hardware jig. “Root access required” means the device needs administrator-level permission before that action can be done. In this thread, rooting the Xperia P is described as a way to get that access, and it can be done without unlocking the bootloader. “Root Access Required” means you need administrator-level permission on the device before you can make certain system changes.

In this context, it’s needed because stock devices usually block full filesystem access and only allow manufacturer-approved updates. For persistent usage, check:
du -d 1 -h /data/app

That’s where the APKs themselves are stored.

su

adb devices

`adb shell ime` is the command to look at, not `adb` itself. `adb shell ime` supports:

`ime list [-a] [-s]`
`ime enable ID`
`ime disable ID`
`ime set ID`

If `ime set` gives `Unknown ID: null`, that means the IME ID you passed wasn’t valid or wasn’t found. Use `adb shell ime list -a` to see all IME IDs, then copy one exactly and use it with `ime set ID`.

`ime list -s` shows only a short summary of enabled IMEs; `ime list` shows enabled IMEs with more detail. If both return nothing, there may be no enabled IMEs on the device.

The IME ID must include both the package and the service/class name, not just the class name. For example:

adb shell ime enable com.thihaayekyaw.frozenkeyboard/com.example.android.softkeyboard.SoftKeyboard
adb shell ime set com.thihaayekyaw.frozenkeyboard/com.example.android.softkeyboard.SoftKeyboard

Also, `ime enable` only makes the IME available; `ime set` is what actually selects it as the active input method. If you see “Unknown ID: null,” it likely means the ID you passed was incomplete or not the exact `package/service` ID shown by `ime list -a`.

To install an APK as a system app, you generally need to place it on the system partition, not install it normally. Copy it to /system/app or, on Android 4.3+, /system/priv-app using adb.

You may need to remount /system read-write first:

adb shell
su
mount -o rw,remount /system

Or from the host:

adb root
adb remount

Then push or move the APK there, set permissions to rw-r--r-- (chmod 644 /path_to_file), and reboot the device.

Rooting gives an app root privileges, which means it can use the entire system, including facilities that normally require app permissions. In principle, a rooted app can also modify the permissions database to grant its non-root part additional permissions beyond what was requested at install time. So the access comes from trusted root-level control over the system, not from the app legitimately adding itself to a normal permission group.

Programmatically, rooting works by first getting past bootloader protection so the system partition can be written. That may involve exploiting a vulnerability, flashing a new bootloader or recovery, or using an official unlock method.

Then the root binaries are installed, usually the su binary plus a small app that manages requests for superuser access. su is the program that elevates an app’s permissions when invoked.

So the “magic” is not a permanent change to every app’s privileges; it’s that the device is modified to allow a controlled path to superuser access, and apps ask for it through su.

If your HTC Butterfly has no OS and is stuck in bootloader/recovery, the supported fix here is to use fastboot from the Android SDK.

Example:
adb shell su -c 'sqlite3 /data/data/<YOUR_LAUNCHER>/databases/<DB_FILE> "DELETE FROM <TABLE>"'

For some stock launchers:
adb shell su -c 'sqlite3 /data/data/com.android.launcher/databases/launcher.db "DELETE FROM favorites"'

You’ll need to identify the correct launcher database and table first, since it can vary. Use sqlite3 .tables and .schema, or inspect the DB with a SQLite editor/DB Browser.

A downloaded .apk is usually installed as a normal app in /data/app on internal memory. Apps on external storage are kept in an encrypted container under /mnt/sdcard/.android_secure, with a decrypted runtime copy in /mnt/asec. App data is separate, typically under /data/data/<package_name>. System/preinstalled apps are in /system/app, and privileged ones in /system/priv-app. If the APK was installed with adb install or downloaded from Market, it generally won’t remain as a recognizable .apk in the same place you downloaded it from.
Downloaded .apk files are stored in subfolders under /data on the device. By default, you don’t have permission to read that location. To access it, you would need to root the phone.

The supported approach here is to set up a cross-compiling toolchain from the Android NDK, not to install a full GNU build environment directly on the device.

Use `build/tools/make-standalone-toolchain.sh` from the NDK and pass `--install-dir=...` to create a standalone toolchain, for example:

`build/tools/make-standalone-toolchain.sh --install-dir=/tmp/android-standalone-toolchain`

Then add its `bin` directory to your `PATH` and configure projects for cross-compiling, e.g.:

`./configure --target=arm-linux-androideabi --host=arm-linux-androideabi`

After that, run `make`. This only covers compiling for Android/ARM; it doesn’t explain how to install Android built from source onto a bare device.

It’s doing dex optimization for installed apps. In practice, during the first boot after the update, Android loops through apps, shows “Optimizing application,” and runs performDexOpt on them so their bytecode is prepared for the new system version. In other words, it’s not changing the apps themselves so much as recompiling/optimizing them for faster loading after the upgrade.

The evidence says your network is probably fine if you can browse/play UPnP content. The key issue is that browsing a DMS (“pull”) is separate from receiving pushed content from a DMC/DMS (“push”), and many Android DMR apps do not implement the push-capable AVTransport functions.

For diagnosis, use Intel UPnP Developer Tools’ DeviceSpy on Windows and check whether the MK802 exposes AVTransport, especially SetAVTransportURI. If AVTransport isn’t present, it won’t receive push media.

It also notes that common Android apps like BubbleUPnP and UPnPPlay did not implement push. You may need to try other DMR apps from the wiki list, but the evidence doesn’t name a working one for Android 4.2.2 on MK802.

Based on the evidence, Android does not hide RAM from you in the sense of “used” RAM cells draining more battery. The hardware doesn’t distinguish between RAM holding data and RAM that looks empty, so RAM usage itself is not a direct battery drain.

What matters more is CPU activity. Keeping apps in memory is usually fine, and Android manages resources well. Killing apps can actually cost more battery because they may need to be restarted later. If an app is constantly using CPU, that can drain battery, but that’s about the app’s behavior, not hidden RAM.

Not from the device RAM itself. The evidence only shows that you cannot “expand your RAM” by using an SD card; instead, you can create swap space on the SD card, which is slower than RAM and requires root. It does not say Android hides a portion of RAM from the user.

Android does not normally “hide” RAM from the user in the paging-to-disk sense. It typically does not use swap/virtual memory that transparently moves less-used data out of RAM by default.

Instead, when RAM is needed, Android frees it by terminating cached apps, after giving them a chance to save state. It also uses virtual memory internally in the Linux/MMU sense, so apps have virtual addresses and are isolated from each other.

So the closest answer is: Android may reserve some memory for the system and uses RAM management internally, but it generally doesn’t hide user RAM by paging app data to storage.

The best pre-theft practice is to encrypt the device, install anti-theft software that can track or remotely wipe it, and make sure Google’s Device Manager is enabled and actually working. For the best chance of recovering it or photographing the thief, an app like GotYa! Face Trap can take a photo after failed logins, provided the device has a front camera. Also keep important data backed up off-device, for example with cloud sync or your own computer, and consider encrypting cloud-stored data as well.

The best practice mentioned is to use software that can remotely track and wipe your phone, such as Mobile Defense. The thread also suggests securing the phone itself, for example by adding a password for unlocking it.

If the phone wasn’t linked, or your contacts were saved locally, there’s no way to recover them from Google.

The other relevant point is that Android has an API method, setMaximumFailedPasswordsForWipe(), but the material here does not confirm a built-in user interface that calls it. If you need this behavior on that device, Autowipe is the supported option shown here.

For bloatware, freezing is the safer option: it doesn’t uninstall the app, just hides it and stops it from running. It’s fully reversible and doesn’t touch the app’s data. A good way is to freeze one app first and check for side effects before freezing more.

Removing apps is permanent unless you have a backup to restore from.

There’s no official way to install “pure Android” on a rooted tablet; the only official ROM is the manufacturer’s. The main caveats are:
- avoid low-quality car chargers or noisy power sources
- make sure the charger is a proper USB charger with the right output
- if the plug/cable is unusual, use the correct cable

So using another phone’s charger is typically safe and shouldn’t affect the phone in any harmful way.

Yes—GPS itself works without internet or 3G. It’s passive and receives satellite signals directly.

So if GPS seems not to work with 3G off, it may just be taking longer to acquire a lock rather than needing internet.

The working steps were:
- connect Android to the PC by USB
- enable tethering so usb0 appears
- enable Wi‑Fi hotspot
- on Android, get USB networking up with:
  netcfg usb0 dhcp
  busybox route add default gw 10.42.0.1 dev usb0
- disable mobile data if needed
- enable forwarding and NAT:
  echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
  iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o usb0 -j MASQUERADE
  iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT

Phones use limited user rights for safety. On Android, each app runs under its own user, which helps enforce permissions and limits what a compromised app can do. It can’t just be copied because the `su` binary needs special permissions to work correctly: the accepted answer says it must be owned/permissioned with the setuid/setgid bits, shown as `-rwsr-sr-x`, so that it runs with the file owner/group’s privileges rather than the caller’s.

A plain copy would not preserve those permissions unless you set them again afterward. The answer says to use `chmod` to restore them, specifically:

`chmod 6774 su`

That sets the special bits and execute permissions matching the displayed mode.

`adb shell su` runs `su` as a single command and then returns to the shell. It does not create an interactive root session by itself, so further commands won’t keep flowing through that same invocation.

What you want is to start an interactive shell first with `adb shell`, then run `su` inside that shell. If the device requires it, you may also need to grant superuser permission depending on boot.img/kernel configuration.

For `ddmlib`, `device.executeShellCommand("su", receiver)` is likely hitting the same issue: it executes only `su` and may not produce a usable interactive session, which can lead to `ShellCommandUnresponsiveException`.

It can’t always be “simply copied” because getting the su binary onto the device in the first place depends on the device. Some devices have vulnerabilities that let you push su with adb, but others do not. In those cases, flashing a rooted ROM or another rooting method is required to place su on the system.

So the short answer is: on some devices you can copy it via an exploit; on others you can’t, because no such access exists. It depends on your device.

In Android usage, USB host mode and OTG are often treated as the same thing.

Host mode means the device is acting as the USB host, controlling connected peripherals. OTG is the feature that lets a phone/tablet switch roles and operate as a host when needed, instead of only as a peripheral.

So for charging: if the device is in host mode, it is typically supplying power to the attached USB device, not charging itself. Whether it can still charge while hosting depends on the specific device and hardware support, which this answer doesn’t cover.

If you have a terminal emulator, root, and busybox, you can mount the flash drive manually:

1. Open terminal.
2. Type `su` to get root.
3. Insert the USB cable and flash drive.
4. Use `dmesg` to find the device name.
5. Create a folder to use as a mount point.
6. Mount it with a command like:
   `mount -t ext4 /dev/(device name) (path to folder)`
7. `cd` into that folder.
8. If needed, change permissions with `chmod 777 (your file)`.

After that, you can access it through a file manager. If you only need a simpler method, StickMount was suggested as an alternative.

The Android terminal emulator uses BusyBox Linux, so you should use BusyBox commands. The suggested command for formatting is:

fdformat DEVICE

For example:
fdformat /dev/sdcard

This is the only specific formatting command given, and it may depend on the exact device path. If you’re not sure of the correct device name for your flash drive, you’d need to identify it first before running the command.

Link2SD uses a second SD card partition so apps can stay available even when the main SD card is mounted to a PC over USB mass storage. If it used the only partition, apps could disappear while the card is shared. A separate partition also lets it use ext3/ext4 instead of FAT, which is better for linking and performance. Using the only partition would also create compatibility problems for Windows, since Windows doesn’t support EXT filesystems out of the box.

To make the SD partition primary, the supported method here is to use Windows DiskPart. Back up the SD card first, then in DiskPart choose the SD card, run clean to remove existing partitions, and create a new partition with:

create partition primary

If you want a smaller one, add size=100 for 100 MB. Then select the partition and format it, for example:

format fs=fat32 label="SDCARD"

This guidance covers creating a primary partition from scratch, not converting an existing logical partition directly.

If it’s an external SD card, remove it from the phone and use an SD card reader or USB adapter on your Linux laptop. Then partition it with a tool like gparted. Make sure to choose the correct filesystem(s).

A typical Android boot goes like this: first the Boot ROM runs from hardware and finds the first-stage bootloader in RAM. Then the bootloader starts and hands off to the Linux kernel. The kernel, together with init, brings up basic system parts like file systems and caches. Next, Zygote starts and initializes the Dalvik VM. After that, System Server starts Android services such as telephony and Bluetooth. Finally, Android broadcasts “boot completed,” and apps that listen for that event can start.

Fastboot and recovery are bootloader-related modes/tools. The two boot animations you saw are likely from the device vendor first, then from the Android ROM, before the lock screen appears.

Then restart ADB:

adb kill-server

If Windows still shows a warning or doesn’t recognize it, uninstall the Fire in Device Manager, unplug it, and plug it back in so the driver can reinstall.

In Android 4.2, /sdcard was changed because of multi-user support. The “sdcard” storage became user-scoped, so the primary user’s files are mapped to /sdcard/0 (also /storage/emulated/0). /sdcard/legacy was kept as a compatibility path for apps expecting the old layout. The old single shared /sdcard model was replaced by per-user directories, so what you’re seeing is expected.

In Android 4.2, the storage path changed as part of the move to multi-user support. The old “/sdcard” now points to user 0’s emulated storage, so you may see it as /sdcard/0/ or /storage/emulated/0/. It’s not that the SD card itself changed; it’s the internal shared storage being separated per user. This also fits with the note that /storage/sdcard0 was vfat and mounted as internal storage, not a real removable card.

The difference is because RAM and device memory do different jobs. RAM is temporary working memory: when you open an app, it gets loaded into RAM so it can run quickly, and background apps may stay there too. Device memory is your phone’s built-in storage for files and system data, so it holds what’s saved on the phone even when power is off. That’s why RAM usage can change a lot and quickly, while device memory usage is more permanent. On newer Android phones, part of internal storage may also be shown as an “emulated SD card,” which can make the numbers seem confusing.

The difference is because the advertised 3 GB is the total memory installed in the device, but not all of it is available to Android. Some RAM is shared or reserved for other components like the GPU and modem/baseband. So Android may only report about 2.4 GB available to the application processor. The missing ~0.6 GB isn’t gone; it’s being used elsewhere in the system.

Because on many Android devices RAM is both constrained by hardware and not always usable the way a PC would use it. The answer notes that RAM is costly in more than just chip price: it also needs buses, power, controller support, space, and it increases battery drain. More RAM can also be wasted if the system keeps memory filled to save CPU cycles.

It also says 32-bit processors limit usable address space to 4 GB total, including RAM plus device-mapped hardware, so practical RAM is around 3 GB or less. So “little unused RAM” is often normal: Android keeps RAM full on purpose, and extra RAM may not be economical or fully addressable.

The “missing” RAM isn’t actually gone. The 3 GB advertised is the total memory installed in the device, but some of it is shared with other components like the AP, BP, and GPU. Android only reports the amount available to the application processor, which is about 2.4 GB in this case. So the lower unused/free RAM you see is normal, and the rest is being used elsewhere in the device rather than by apps or the OS cache.

Disabling some apps can help reduce RAM use, especially pre-installed bloatware that runs background services and may not get killed by the low-memory manager. That frees memory for other processes and can reduce the chance of apps being closed because of low memory. 

How much you notice depends on your device’s RAM: on low-RAM devices it may make a bigger difference, while with 2 GB or more you might not notice much beyond possible battery benefits.

With 512 MB RAM, ICS can still be usable, and one user reported no general problems on an LG Optimus 2X. The main issue mentioned was that memory-hungry apps like Chrome can feel a bit laggy. So the evidence suggests 512 MB RAM is not automatically a problem for everyday use, but heavier apps may show performance issues.

Android uses free RAM to keep apps ready in the background, so low free RAM by itself is normal. Closing apps or using a task killer just kills background apps; it doesn’t create “extra” usable memory without tradeoffs. The closest supported advice is to stop unwanted apps and services from running, or accept that Android will reuse RAM this way. If you want more drastic changes, you’d need a custom ROM that changes Android’s memory management, or possibly a swap partition.

Rooting, recovery, and custom ROMs are different things.

Rooting gives administrator-like access so apps can change system files.
Recovery is a special boot mode for installing updates, wiping data, and making backups.
A custom recovery is often needed to flash a custom ROM.
A custom ROM is a replacement Android system, and it may already be rooted.

So, if you want to install a custom ROM, you usually need a custom recovery, and rooting is separate. Once a custom ROM and recovery are installed, you generally don’t repeat rooting or bootloader-unlock steps for every update.

To back up before installing a custom ROM, use a Nandroid backup in recovery. Reboot into recovery, open Backup/Restore, and choose Backup. This saves an exact copy of the phone’s current state, including settings and home screen widgets. After installing the custom ROM, return to recovery and choose Restore to put the phone back exactly as it was.

How you enter recovery depends on the phone. Common methods include holding Volume Down at boot, or on a rooted phone using Power > Reboot/Recovery.

To copy an installed app’s APK from your phone to your PC, use ADB:

1. Find the app’s package name:
`adb shell pm list packages`

2. Get the APK path:
`adb shell pm path my.package.name`

3. Pull the APK to your computer:
`adb pull /data/app/my.package.name`

To back up APKs from a phone to a PC, use ADB:

1. Find the app package name:
`adb shell pm list packages`

2. Get the APK path:
`adb shell pm path your.package.name`

3. Pull the APK to your computer:
`adb pull /data/app/your.package.name`

This is the closest supported method provided. If you want to back up all installed APKs, you would need to repeat this for each package name.

If you’re changing SD cards, copy everything from the old card to the new one, including hidden files and folders. That’s the safest way to keep any app data that was stored on the card.

Steps:
1. Power off the phone.
2. Remove the old SD card and connect it to a PC.
3. Copy all files and directories to a folder on the PC.
4. Safely unmount the old card.
5. Insert the new SD card and copy everything from the PC to it, including hidden items.
6. Safely unmount it, put it back in the phone, and turn the phone on.

This doesn’t explain moving apps from internal storage to SD card, but it does cover transferring card contents when switching cards.

An Android ROM is device-specific because manufacturers modify Android and the kernel to match the hardware in that exact device. Different phones have different drivers and hardware features, so changes that work on one device may not work on another. For example, a feature like voice recording may depend on device-specific drivers in a manufacturer’s kernel and wouldn’t work in a more generic AOSP build unless it’s adapted for that hardware.

An Android ROM is device-specific because manufacturers’ interfaces and modifications are usually proprietary and tied to particular hardware. A ROM made for one phone generally cannot be flashed onto another phone and work properly. There have been attempts to port interfaces like Samsung TouchWiz or HTC Sense to other devices, but they’re unstable and not meant for everyday use.

So the closest supported answer is: you usually need a ROM made for your exact device, or at least one specifically ported to it.

adb pull /data/app/my.package.name

That’s generally normal. Android/Linux try to use as much RAM as possible for caching and other performance improvements, so “unused” RAM is not really something you want to see. If apps need more memory, those caches are cleared first. So a higher “used” RAM number after the upgrade does not necessarily mean something is wrong.

If Android shows very little free RAM, that does not necessarily mean the RAM is missing or a problem. The advertised 3 GB is the total installed memory, but some of it is shared with other components such as the GPU and other hardware. Android may only report about 2.4 GB as available to the main processor, with the rest reserved elsewhere. So “0 RAM free” or low free RAM can be normal, especially if the device is managing memory by using cache and reserved allocations.

An Android factory reset returns the device to its factory state and can help if slow performance is caused by accumulated data or settings. It wipes user data on writable storage, including installed apps, accounts, and personal data, but it does not erase the read-only system partition. That means pre-installed/uninstallable apps should remain intact after the reset. It also will not revert a device with system updates back to its original Android version. Back up anything important first.

A factory reset removes personal settings, data, and installed apps, but it does not remove the Android OS update itself. So if your phone was upgraded, a factory reset will usually keep the newer Android version and not revert to the original one. To go back to an older version, you would need to reflash or reinstall an older firmware image from the manufacturer or carrier.
